supplementary_info.identification_information: 28-31 cm. Metallic glossy green upperparts with blackish crest and bronze scapulars. Very broad wings, especially primaries and most exaggerated in breeding males. Non-breeding adult with buff face, white chin and throat, while the upperwing-coverts and scapulars have buff fringes. Juvenile similar to non-breeding adult but with broader buff fringes (Wiersma et al. 2020).

documentation.range: The species breeds from Europe, Türkiye and north-west Iran through western Russia and Kazakhstan to southern and eastern Siberia, Mongolia and northern China. It winters from western Europe, the east Atlantic islands and North Africa through the Mediterranean, Middle East and Iran across northern India to south-east China, the Korean peninsula and southern Japan (Wiersma et al. 2020).
documentation.population: The global population, which is considered to comprise three flyway populations, is estimated to number 6,400,000-10,500,000 individuals (Wetlands International 2023). Using the standard factor to convert numbers of waterbirds from individuals to mature individuals (0.67), this equates to approximately 4,300,000-7,000,000 mature individuals.
documentation.habitats: The species shows a preference for breeding on wet natural grasslands, meadows and hay meadows with short swards and patches of bare soil at low altitudes of mostly less than 1,000 m (Johnsgard 1981, Hayman et al. 1986, del Hoyo et al. 1996, Snow and Perrins 1998, Trolliet 2003, Devereux et al. 2004). It will also breed on grassy moors, swampy heaths, bogs and arable fields (Johnsgard 1981, del Hoyo et al. 1996). The nest is a shallow scrape in short grass vegetation (del Hoyo et al. 1996). During the winter the species utilises large open pastures for roosting and forages on damp grassland, irrigated land, stubble and ploughed fields, riverbanks, lake shores, fresh and saline marshes, drainage ditches, estuaries and mudflats (Africa) (Urban et al. 1986, del Hoyo et al. 1996). Its diet consists of adult and larval insects (e.g. beetles, ants, Diptera, crickets, grasshoppers, dragonflies, mayflies, cicadas and Lepidoptera), spiders, snails, earthworms, frogs, small fish (Africa) and seeds or other plant material (Africa) (Urban et al. 1986, del Hoyo et al. 1996). Most populations of this species are fully migratory and travel on a broad front out of Europe although some breeding populations in more temperate regions are sedentary (del Hoyo et al. 1996, Snow and Perrins 1998). The species breeds from April to July in solitary pairs although pairs may also nest close together in optimal habitat (Johnsgard 1981, Hayman et al. 1986, del Hoyo et al. 1996, Trolliet 2003).
documentation.threats:
This species suffered past declines as a result of land-use intensification, wetland drainage and egg collecting (del Hoyo et al. 1996). The main threats facing this species today is low productivity from habitat loss and degradation on breeding grounds, and predation. Productivity of approximately > 0.8 fledglings per pairs would be required to stabilise and sustain populations, however rates of reproduction are low, such as 0.23 in England (Rickenbach et al. 2011), or 0.46 in the Netherlands (Plard et al. 2020). Land-use intensification reduces breeding productivity by intensifying and changing agricultural practices (del Hoyo et al. 1996), especially the improvement of grasslands (e.g. by drainage, application of inorganic fertilizers and reseeding) (Baldi et al. 2005, Düttmann et al. 2018), increased growing of "winter-crops" (see Eggers et al. 2011), and loss of field margins and semi-natural habitat. Important migratory stop-over habitats for this species on the Baltic Sea coastline are threatened by petroleum pollution, wetland drainage for irrigation, land abandonment and changing land management practices leading to scrub overgrowth (Grishanov 2006). Clutch destruction may also occur during spring cultivation (using machinery) on arable fields (del Hoyo et al. 1996). Certain habitats are believed to be ecological or anthropogenic traps, such as the coincident timing of nesting periods and farming operations in maize fields in Slovenia (Horvat and Denac 2019), or agricultural landscapes in Ukraine (Shydlovskyy and Kuzyo 2016). The species is susceptible to avian botulism so may be threatened by future outbreaks of the disease (Hubalek et al. 2005). Avian influenza may be an additional threat.

Predation and nest predation by native and introduced predators has a significant impact on productivity and there is evidence that populations of some nest predators have increased as a result of human changes to ecosystems (Macdonald and Bolton 2008). Predators include Red Fox Vulpes vulpes, Eurasian Badger Meles meles, Eurasian Otter Lutra lutra, Carrion Crow Corvus corone, Herring Gull Larus argentatus, Greater Black-backed Gull Larus marinus, Lesser Black-backed Gull Larus fuscus, Grey Heron Ardea cinerea, Marsh Harrier Circus aeruginosus (M. Sorrenti in litt. 2016, Bertholdt et al. 2017); and the European Hedgehog Erinaceus europeaus where introduced on some islands (Jackson 2001). A study in the UK identified raptors as being primarily responsible for predation by birds and Red Fox for predation by mammals, with foxes also having a larger influence on daily chick predation rates than other predators (Mason et al. 2018). Chick predation also increased seasonally, suggesting earlier breeding attempts would be more successful. 

The species is hunted for commercial use (to be sold as food) and for recreational purposes in Iran (Balmaki and Barati 2006), and is hunted in France, Greece, Italy and Spain (Trolliet 2003): population impacts of the current level of take are not well quantified.
documentation.measures:
Conservation and Research Actions Underway
CMS Appendix II. EU Birds Directive Annex II.  Bern Convention Annex III. A European management plan was published in 2009 (Petersen 2009), updated with an International Multi-species Action Plan for the conservation of breeding waders in Europe (Leyrer et al. 2018). Management of habitat for this species occurs in several European countries and agro-environment schemes are in place in France, the Netherlands and the U.K. (Petersen 2009) although they have been shown to not always be effective (Breeuwer et al. 2009).  

Conservation and Research Actions Proposed
Continue research to find the most appropriate land management practices for this, and other species (e.g. Chiron et al. 2010, Eggers et al. 2011, Peach et al. 2011, MacDonald et al. 2012). Develop management schemes to reduce predation as well as monitoring and research programmes to inform conservation measures (Petersen 2009). Record reliable bag statistics.
Visible marking of wader nests to avoid damage by farmers does not increase nest predation and so is a suitable option to consider (Zamecnik et al. 2018). Ensure incentives are in place for landowners to restore and manage suitable habitat as well as reduce pesticide use, reduce livestock densities and postpone first cut, which will support survival of nests and chicks. The improvement of chick habitat can include promoting heterogeneous swards combining tall vegetation for hiding and short and open vegetation for foraging (Plard et al. 2020). Raising and maintaining high water levels until mid-summer ensures the penetrability of the soil surface and provides sufficient prey for adults and chicks (Düttmann et al. 2018). Due to its long-term adverse effects on density and reproduction of Northern Lapwings, grassland renewal should not be practiced in areas with conservation responsibilities for grassland-breeding waders (Düttmann et al. 2018). Reduce hunting pressure and create awareness campaigns, targeted at hunters, about the decline of this species.
documentation.use_trade: This species has been reported as used in trade at a high prevalence, being found in three of the seven trade datasets evaluated (Donald et al. 2024). Historical declines in the western populations of the species may have been partly driven by egg collecting (del Hoyo et al. 1996). The species is hunted for commercial use (to be sold as food) and for recreational purposes in Iran (Balmaki and Barati 2006), and is hunted in France, Greece, Italy, Spain and Malta (Trolliet 2003).
documentation.rationale: Although this species remains widespread and still has a large global population, numbers have declined rapidly in some parts of its range over recent decades. Overall, the global population is estimated to be declining at rate of 20-29% over three generations. The species therefore qualifies as Near Threatened.
documentation.trend_justification: The overall population trend is decreasing, although the populations in Asia have an unknown trend (Wetlands International 2023). In Europe, the large breeding population has decreased at a rate exceeding 30% over three generations, particularly in the European Union (PECBMS 2023), resulting in its assessment as Vulnerable at both EU and European levels (BirdLife International 2021). However, the EU only holds around half of the European population, and in European Russia (holding another third) declines have been slower, while in Belarus (with c. 15%) the population appears to be stable, with increases noted in both in Finland and Estonia (BirdLife International 2021). The rate of reduction has been higher in the western part of the range, where habitat loss and degradation due to agricultural intensification have been most intense (Leyrer et al. 2018). Although trend data are lacking, populations breeding farther east (in southern Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia and northern China) are therefore considered more likely to be stable or declining slowly, compared to the more rapid declines in western Europe. Acknowledging this uncertainty, the overall rate of reduction over three generations is considered most likely to fall between 20-29%.
